centralObject.name: The Ratepayer Protection Act, H.R. 9340 — a large-load cost standard states must consider under PURPA, which failed to advance in the Senate 57-43 on 2026-09-30

place.why: After the vote nothing is in force, and even passage would have produced only a PURPA 111(d) consider-and-determine duty with no binding cost rule, so the instrument mainly presses on the institutional blocs: Republicans who sold it as price relief and Democrats who sank a 417-3 bill for one that can't pass a 53-47 Senate.

tethers.title: Ratepayer Protection Act
tethers.statusAsOf: 2026-09-30: failed to advance in the Senate, 57-43 with 60 needed (Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff, Warnock yes); House-passed 2026-09-16, 417-3; on the Senate calendar (No. 684) since 2026-09-24
tethers.why: The instrument itself: adds a 'Standards for Large-Load Customers' standard to PURPA §111(d) that state regulators and non-regulated utilities must consider — whether customers of 100 MW or more pay the full incremental cost of grid upgrades, with financial assurance up front.

place.why: Same instrument as the central object.

tethers.statute: Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 (PURPA), §111(d)
tethers.title: PURPA's consider-and-determine standards
tethers.why: The legacy mechanism H.R. 9340 rides: states must hold a proceeding and decide on each federal standard, but need not adopt it. The bill's whole delivery question is this statute's design.

place.why: The 1978 vehicle, not the instrument; it neither delivers nor fails on this vote.

tethers.why: The Democrats' alternative named on the floor 09-30: FERC would set binding interconnection rules making large new users pay for the grid upgrades they need. The 'real teeth' the no votes cited.

place.why: A rival text that never became the instrument; it neither delivers nor fails.

title: Asked to Consider
prompt: The Senate blocked a bill to keep data center costs off household electric bills. Does a standard states only have to consider protect anyone?
framing: On Wednesday, September 30, 2026, the Senate voted 57 to 43 to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340), short of the 60 votes needed. Four Democrats voted yes: Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock. The House passed the bill 417 to 3 on September 16, 2026. It would require state regulators to consider whether data centers and other customers drawing 100 megawatts or more should pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they need. Each state decides whether to adopt it. On the day of the vote, Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said the bill lets Republicans prove they are "for lower electricity prices," and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it "a fraud." Democrats back Sen. Martin Heinrich's GRID Savings Act (introduced August 3, 2026), which would require it.

split.seam: Whether state discretion plus voluntary pledges count as protection, or whether only a binding rule that makes the big users pay does.
split.rationale: Most stations read the bill as non-delivering. The right-institutional quadrant peels off positive on trust in states and governors, joined weakly by the left-institutional coalition speaker who prefers a passable floor and the right-populist coalition speaker who prefers the statehouse to Washington. The populist rims sit deep negative on distrust of Big Tech.

zPattern.note: Centers are fluid z; coalition z: A +0.2, B −0.15, C −0.45, D +0.1. Three of four coalitions cross their own fluid sign (A and D up through zero, B down through it). Rims sign by holder-trust exactly: B's rim trusts the Republican governors; A, C and D rims distrust Husted's party, Big Tech, or the tech billionaires.

antiValentRationale: In the coalition band signs run against each quadrant's tendency: A crosses to positive (taking the floor its own party blocked), B drops below zero (doubting the pledge its side leans on), and D crosses to positive (statehouse over Washington). Weighing their own side's tactic is what flips them.

z.pos: the bill delivers: data centers end up paying their own grid costs, household bills are protected, and this vote moves that closer
z.neg: it doesn't: a standard states only have to consider, with nothing to make data centers pay; no protection comes of it

fluid.zReason: Under PURPA 111(d) a commission has to hold a proceeding and rule on the large-load standard, but it can say no, so any cost shifting depends entirely on each state choosing it.
fluid.text: I know how 111(d) works: the commission has to open a docket, take comment, and write down a decision. That isn't nothing, because it puts data center cost allocation on the record in every state. But a commission that's already friendly to the data center can just decline, so I can't call it protection for my bill.

coalition.zReason: Forcing every commission to rule on the question is a real, passable step, and blocking it for the GRID Savings Act gives up that step for a bill with no path in a 53-47 Senate.
coalition.text: The people I vote with killed a bill the House passed 417 to 3 so they could hold out for Heinrich's version, and Heinrich's version isn't getting 60 votes either. Hassan, Klobuchar, Ossoff and Warnock looked at that math and took the docket in every state. I think they're right. A weak floor beats an empty room.

denominated.zReason: The speaker reads the bill as a Republican campaign device and distrusts its sponsors to deliver anything to ratepayers.
denominated.text: It's Jon Husted's ad for November. I don't trust anything his side needs to pass five weeks before an election.

fluid.zReason: The standard puts large-load cost recovery in front of every state regulator while leaving the decision with states, and it works alongside the pledge companies already signed to pay for their own upgrades.
fluid.text: This is the right shape for it: it adds a standard to a law that's been around since 1978 and lets each state's regulators decide what fits their grid. Add the pledge, where the big tech companies already said they'd cover their own upgrades, and the direction is clear. It didn't clear 60 today, but 57 senators and nearly the whole House want this.

coalition.zReason: Without a binding rule, protection rests on a voluntary pledge from the same companies the President wants building faster, and nothing enforces it.
coalition.text: I like the bill, but the people I vote with keep pointing at the pledge as if it settles the question. It's voluntary, and the White House wants these data centers built as fast as possible. If Husted needs this to prove he's for lower prices, I'd want it to actually make somebody pay.

denominated.zReason: The speaker trusts Republican governors and state leadership to make data centers pay without Washington ordering it.
denominated.text: Twenty-three Republican governors already signed on. Leave it to them.

fluid.zReason: A standard regulators only have to consider leaves cost allocation with commissions and utilities that have every reason to keep data centers happy, so nothing makes the 100-megawatt users pay.
fluid.text: Consider? My electric bill doesn't get considered, it gets paid. This hands the question to the same state commissions that approved the rate hikes, and lets them shrug. Without a rule that makes the big users pay, it's toothless.

coalition.zReason: The Democratic alternative also can't pass, so blocking this one only means no rule at all while bills keep rising.
coalition.text: Schumer's right that this bill is weak. But the people I vote with blocked it and their real bill isn't moving either, so what do I get in the meantime? A fraud on one side and a press release on the other, and my bill still goes up.

denominated.zReason: The speaker trusts no instrument that depends on Big Tech's good faith.
denominated.text: Big Tech never pays for anything it can push onto everybody else. I don't believe that changes.

fluid.zReason: Making the full-cost standard optional and relying on voluntary pledges lets the tech companies decide whether they pay, and nothing obliges them to.
fluid.text: I don't want these data centers in my county, and I sure don't want to pay for their power lines. A standard my state can just ignore doesn't stop that. The companies promising to pay are the same ones who've never paid for anything they could dodge.

coalition.zReason: A state-decided standard keeps the fight at the statehouse, where voters can push, instead of handing it to federal regulators under Heinrich's bill.
coalition.text: The people I vote with sold this as more than it is, and the President wants every data center built yesterday, so I don't buy that it's a cure. But Heinrich's bill hands the whole thing to regulators in Washington. I'd rather fight it out in my own statehouse, so I'll take the weak version.

denominated.zReason: The speaker reads the bill as cover for tech billionaires and distrusts them to protect anyone's bill.
denominated.text: It's the tech billionaires' bill wearing a red jersey. They're not paying my light bill.

objectLayer.stated: A ratepayer protection: data centers of 100 MW or more pay the full incremental cost of the grid upgrades they need, so household bills don't carry it.
objectLayer.operative: A PURPA §111(d) consider-and-determine duty: every state commission must open a proceeding and rule on the standard, and may reject it. The vote was over whether a duty to consider counts as protection; 57 said yes, and the no votes, by their own account, held out for a binding FERC rule (GRID Savings Act) that has no visible path.
objectLayer.inversion: Lean, not ruled: a chamber flip on the left, not a z flip. House Democrats voted for the bill almost unanimously on 2026-09-16 (417-3); 43 of 47 Senate Democrats voted no on 09-30. On the right, D-fluid reads against its own party's bill on Big Tech distrust, while the president backs data center buildout. See meta.newsroomFindings.
